God swears at the opening of the surah by the dawn, by the ten nights, by the even and the odd, and by the night as it passes. The commentators agree that the dawn is the familiar break of day, but they differ on what the oath refers to. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali and Ibn al-Zubayr take it as the dawn that returns each day, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid as the dawn of the day of sacrifice, al-Dahhak as the dawn of the first day of dhu al-hijja, and others as the whole day or the dawn prayer.

Regarding the ten nights, most, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak, identify them as the first ten nights of dhu al-hijja. Others propose the last ten nights of Ramadan, the first ten of Muharram, or the ten nights of Moses' appointment. Al-Tabari holds that they are the ten days of sacrifice, and Ibn Kathir accepts this while noting doubts about the wording of the report that raises it to the Prophet.

The even and the odd have received many interpretations. According to Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima, the even is the day of sacrifice and the odd is the day of 'Arafat. Ibn al-Zubayr identifies them with the two days after the sacrifice and the third day. Others take them as all creation, paired and single, with God as the single one, as Mujahid and Abu Salih report. Others read them as the prayers, some even and some odd, as reported from 'Imran ibn Husayn. Al-Tabari did not commit to one view and kept the oath general.

As for the night when it passes, most understand it as its departure, some as its arrival, and Mujahid and 'Ikrima as the night of Muzdalifa. The oath closes with a question that stresses its greatness to the person of intellect, since hijr means reason and restraint.

The commentators explain that « And by ten nights » is an oath sworn by particular nights of great merit. Most identify them as the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja, a view held by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak; some rely on a hadith from Jabir, whose sound transmission al-Tabari accepts while Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari note reservations about its wording. Others, including Ibn 'Abbas according to some reports, identify them as the last ten nights of Ramadan, which Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Uthaymin find the stronger view because of the Night of Decree within them. Yaman ibn Rabab and others say the first ten nights of Muharram.

On the even and the odd, « the even and the odd », the explanations are numerous. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima take them as the day of sacrifice and the day of 'Arafa, others as the days of tashriq, Mujahid and Abu Salih take the even as all creation and the odd as God, 'Imran ibn Husayn and Qatada take them as the prayers, and al-Hasan as numbers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir decline to choose one, and al-Razi holds that the text imposes none.

The night « when it passes » is, for most, the night as it proceeds or departs; Mujahid and 'Ikrima identify it with the night of Muzdalifa. Finally, « Is there in this an oath for one of understanding? » means, according to most, that these oaths suffice for one who has reason and discernment, the hijr being the intellect that restrains a person from what is unseemly.

At the opening of the surah God swears by the dawn, by ten nights, by the even and the odd, and by the night as it passes, then asks, as an emphatic question, whether such oaths suffice for one who has understanding. The commentators agree that these oaths magnify what is sworn by and emphasise the statement that follows. As for the dawn, Ibn Abbas and Ikrima take it as the daybreak of every day, while others take it as the dawn prayer, the dawn of the day of sacrifice, or the whole day. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya favour the familiar dawn.

The ten nights are, according to most, including Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya, the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja, supported by a hadith from Jabir which Ibn Kathir nonetheless considers doubtful in its wording. Others identify them with the first ten days of Muharram or the last ten nights of Ramadan.

The main disagreement concerns the even and the odd. Ibn Abbas and Ikrima hold that the even is the day of sacrifice and the odd the day of Arafat, a view some transmit as a hadith. Ibn al-Zubayr takes it as the two days after the sacrifice and the third day. Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd understand all of creation, pairs and singles, with God as the single. Others, including Ibn Kathir who reports it, read it as prayer, some of which is even and some odd, following a hadith transmitted from Imran ibn Husayn. The passing night is generally understood as night in general, though Mujahid and Ikrima think of the night of Muzdalifa.

Finally, dhu hijr means one who has reason and restraint, since hijr is what holds a person back from what is blameworthy.

In this verse God swears by the night as it passes, that is, as it advances and spreads its darkness, a sign of the Creator's greatness and of the alternation of night and day. The commentators differ on which night is meant. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Kalbi and 'Ikrima took it to be the night of Muzdalifa, when the pilgrims travel. The majority of exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, understood it as any night in general, which al-Qurtubi considered the more apparent meaning. Some grammarians explain the verb yasri as meaning that the night is traversed, as one says a sleeping night, and the readers differ on keeping or dropping the final yā', the omission being explained by the rhythm of the verse endings. On the essentials, the commentators agree that this oath draws attention to the divine power that makes night and day follow one another, and to the blessing of rest that the night brings. Most leave the answer of the oath implied, understood as the punishment of the deniers, which the mention of the destruction of 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh that follows suggests. Al-Tabari and others see this oath as sufficient for anyone endowed with reason.

After the preceding oaths, God in this verse poses a question that is really an affirmation: is there in these things sworn by a sufficient oath for one who has reason and sound judgment? The commentators explain 'hijr' as intellect, reason, forbearance or restraint, its root meaning being prevention, since reason keeps its possessor from what is unseemly. Many read the interrogative as emphatic confirmation rather than a real question, so the sense is that these oaths suffice for the thinking person. On the answer to the oath, opinions differ. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy hold that it is omitted, meaning 'they will surely be punished', which the mention of the destruction of 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh that follows seems to indicate. Ibn al-Anbari takes the answer to be 'indeed your Lord is ever watchful', a view Ibn al-Qayyim finds weak because of the long gap between oath and answer. Muqatil reads 'hal' here as meaning 'inna'. All agree on the purpose: to magnify what is sworn by and to strengthen what is affirmed, which the person of understanding will grasp.

The plain meaning is a question addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, asking whether he has not come to know with certainty how his Lord dealt with 'Ad. The commentators agree that 'Ad was an ancient Arab people, the folk of Hud, famed for their great stature and strength, and that God destroyed them with a wind. They differ over the word "Iram". Mujahid and Qatada take it as the name of the tribe itself, Ibn Ishaq as the forefather of 'Ad, while others take it as the name of a city, which Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and 'Ikrima identify with Damascus and Muhammad ibn Ka'b with Alexandria. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir prefer the sense of a tribe, and Ibn Kathir considers the tales of a golden city of Iram to be Israelite narratives. On "dhat al-'imad", Ibn 'Abbas and al-Zamakhshari understand tall stature, Mujahid understands nomads whose tents rest on poles, Ibn Zayd solid buildings, and al-Dahhak strength. Al-Tabari favours the nomadic or the tall-bodied reading. Ibn Kathir and most commentators agree that mentioning 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh is a warning to the disbelievers, showing that God's power reaches even the strongest peoples.

God reminds His Prophet ﷺ, and every attentive reader, of what He did to the people of 'Ad, called Iram of the pillars, meaning their strength, power and great stature. The verse then turns to Thamud, who hewed rocks in the valley, and to Pharaoh, lord of the stakes, all of whom were tyrannical in their lands and spread corruption there, so their Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment. The commentators generally take Iram to be the name of a tribe of 'Ad or of their forefather, as Qatada, Muqatil, Ibn Ishaq and al-Zajjaj state, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir note that the grammar makes Iram an explanatory apposition to 'Ad, marking them as the earlier 'Ad. Mujahid considered Iram an ancient nation, and al-Dahhak took the word to mean destruction. On the meaning of 'pillars', Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada refer to the great height of the men or to the tent poles of nomads, al-Dahhak to strength, and Ibn Zayd to the solidity of buildings. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Khaldun and others reject the accounts of a golden city of Iram in the deserts of Aden as unfounded. The overall purpose is to warn the disbelievers of Quraysh that God watches over human deeds. On the answer to the oath, Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to be 'Indeed your Lord is ever watchful', while others consider it omitted.

In this verse God addresses His Prophet, through a rhetorical question meant to provoke reflection, about what He did to 'Ad of Iram, a people described as possessing lofty pillars, that is, great strength and tall structures, and of whom it is said that none like them was created in the lands. The commentators agree that 'Ad were the people of Hud and that Iram is the name of their tribe, their forefather or their city. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that Iram is the name of a tribe of 'Ad, and they explain its lack of tanwin by its being a proper name, while Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Juzayy and others understand it as a city or a land. As for the word "pillars", most read it as referring to the great stature of the men, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil; al-Tabari and others mention tents raised on poles among nomads who follow the rains, and Ibn Zayd speaks of buildings with firm columns. The pronoun in "the like of which" refers mostly to the tribe, and some say to the city. Ibn Kathir rejects the accounts of a golden city in the desert as Israelite narratives and finds the chain for Ibn Qilaba unsound, whereas other commentators cite them as reports. Al-Razi explains that "have you not seen" means "have you not known", since these events were widely known among the Arabs.

This verse mentions Thamud, the people of Salih, who hewed out the rock in the valley to make dwellings. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: they carved and hollowed the mountains to make homes for themselves. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi explain that the verb jabu means to cut or pierce, and they relate it to the verse elsewhere saying they carved houses from the mountains in safety. Most identify the valley as the Wadi al-Qura between Medina and Syria, although Ibn Kathir also links it to the site of al-Hijr. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur add that, according to some, Thamud were the first to cut stone and marble, and that they built seventeen hundred cities of stone, a claim Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report without vouching for it. On the grammar, the name Thamud is usually read without tanwin because it is the name of a tribe, while Yahya ibn Wathhab reads it with tanwin as the name of an ancestor. The presence or absence of the final ya in the word for valley is explained by the rhythm of the verse endings. The commentators do not disagree on the general meaning, only on the exact location of the valley and on some details of the traditions.

The commentators explain that the phrase 'and Pharaoh, lord of the stakes' follows the account of 'Ad and Thamud, and it serves to remind the Prophet ﷺ and his listeners of the fate of tyrants who oppressed their lands and spread corruption before God destroyed them. They differ on the meaning of 'dhu al-awtad'. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it to mean his troops and supporters who secured his rule, as tent pegs hold a tent firm; Ibn 'Abbas and others also associate it with the tents and camps pitched for his armies on their journeys. Mujahid, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Kathir report that he tortured people by pegging their hands and feet to stakes, citing his treatment of his wife and of his daughter's hairdresser. Qatada reports that he had terraces and playgrounds supported by stakes. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi record another view, that he had towers or buildings where he punished people. Al-Tabari prefers the ordinary sense of awtad as wooden or iron pegs, since that is the usual meaning of the word. As for the punishment, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir mention drowning, while Qatada and al-Suddi describe various kinds of torment, and al-Zamakhshari reads the 'whip' as a figure for the punishment of this world being slight compared with that of the Hereafter. The commentators conclude with the phrase that your Lord is 'on the watch' over every tyrant, meaning that He observes the deeds of His servants and will repay them.

The commentators explain that this verse continues the account of the tyrannical peoples whom God destroyed: 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh. The phrase "who transgressed in the lands" is taken by most as applying to all of them, or as a qualifier or an expression of blame. For them, transgression means exceeding the limits, rebelling against God's command and opposing His messengers, and this tyranny led to corruption on earth, which brought down God's punishment. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir clarify that "the lands" refers to the territories where these peoples lived, each people having acted tyrannically in its own region. The meaning of "a whip of punishment" varies: al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi see it as an image of the severity of punishment in this world compared to what awaits in the next, while al-Tabari takes it to mean the intensity of the torment, and al-Farra' notes that the Arabs use the phrase for every kind of punishment. The commentators agree that the verse condemns tyranny and warns the deniers of a similar fate, and that "al-mirsad" means God watches over the deeds of His servants to requite them, though they phrase this differently. Al-Razi and al-Tabari note that Iram may be a tribe of 'Ad or a city; most consider it a tribe, while Ibn Kathir judges the identifications with Damascus or Alexandria to be weak.

The commentators explain that the peoples of 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, who acted arrogantly in their lands through disbelief, oppression and disobedience, multiplied corruption there, so their Lord poured down His punishment upon them. Most agree that "corruption" covers disbelief, oppression, killing and all sins. The phrase "a whip of punishment" is taken by some as a kind of torment or its severity, since for the Arabs the whip was the extreme of punishment; al-Zamakhshari adds that mentioning the whip shows that the punishment of this world, however great, is light compared with that of the Hereafter. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri read it as a metaphor for every kind of torment, whereas al-Tabari takes it as a severe chastisement, the whip being a familiar image of beating. On "your Lord is indeed in ambush", Ibn 'Abbas and al-Tabari say He sees and hears; al-Kalbi and al-Suddi say He watches over the disbelievers and sinners so that none escapes Him; al-Hasan and 'Ikrima say He observes the deeds of the children of Adam; al-Dahhak says it concerns the wrongdoers and the disobedient. The commentators also differ over the answer to the oath at the start of the surah: some take it to be "Your Lord is indeed in ambush", while others, such as al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi, supply an implied answer that the context suggests. The passage aims to warn the Quraysh that they may suffer what the earlier peoples suffered, and on this the commentaries agree.

The commentators explain that God sent a severe punishment upon the tyrants of 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, who had spread corruption in the land. On the phrase 'a whip of punishment', views differ. Mujahid and Qatada take it as a kind of torment, or as whatever God used to punish them. Al-Farra' and the scholars of meaning explain that the Arabs used the whip as an image for any kind of torment, since it stood for the limit of pain in their eyes. Al-Zajjaj understands that God made the very whip with which He struck them into the punishment, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya read the construction as a portion of torment. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Biqa'i note that mentioning the whip signals that the punishment of this world is light compared with that of the Hereafter, as a whip is lighter than a sword. As for 'Your Lord is ever watchful', Ibn 'Abbas takes it to mean that God sees and hears, al-Hasan that He watches the deeds of the children of Adam, al-Dahhak that He lies in wait for wrongdoers and the disobedient, Mujahid that all people pass before Him on the Day of Resurrection, and al-Suddi that the Fire has been stationed on their path. Most agree that the verse is a warning to the Quraysh and other oppressors, and that no one escapes God. Ibn Kathir considers the stories of the marvellous city of Iram unsound, a view al-Shawkani also holds.

This verse states that the Lord of the Prophet ﷺ is on watch: nothing people do escapes Him, and He will repay each person for their deeds. The commentators give several meanings to the word al-mirsad. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and those who follow them understand it as God seeing and hearing everything. Al-Hasan and 'Ikrima take it to mean that He observes the deeds of the children of Adam, while al-Kalbi and al-Baghawi say that the path of the servants belongs to Him so that none escapes. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' explain that the word denotes the place where one lies in wait, and that all creation returns to Him. Ad-Dahhak and Muqatil add that God watches over wrongdoers and the disobedient, and that angels are stationed on the Bridge. Al-Zamakhshari sees in the verse a warning aimed at those who defy the Prophet, a reading that Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di link to the threat against the disobedient: God gives them respite and then seizes them. Several reports about the bridges over Hell, where people are questioned about faith, prayer, zakat, fasting, pilgrimage and wrongs done to others, are cited, though Ibn Kathir judges many of them weak. These views converge on one point: nothing escapes God's knowledge and His judgment.

The commentators explain that this verse describes how a person judges his own situation. When God tests him with abundance, he sees it as honour and says, "My Lord has honoured me"; when God restricts his provision, he sees it as humiliation and says, "My Lord has humiliated me". Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that both prosperity and hardship are a trial, and that true honour lies in obeying God. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that a person boasts in prosperity and complains in want, whereas the believer gives thanks in ease and remains patient in hardship.

Most exegetes take the word "al-insan" as referring to humankind in general, though al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani report that the verse was first aimed at certain Meccan notables such as Umayya ibn Khalaf or 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, without limiting its scope. Ibn 'Ashur explains that this judgment reflects the outlook of the polytheists, who measured people's worth by their wealth.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya examine how the passage is structured and the force of the word "kalla", which rejects the belief that wealth proves divine favour. They connect this rejection to the following verses, which censure people for not honouring the orphan, not urging the feeding of the poor, devouring inheritance and loving wealth excessively. Al-Razi offers several reasons for rejecting this belief, notably the brevity of worldly life compared with the hereafter.

Readings differ on a few words, such as "faqadara" with or without the shadda, and on whether the final yā' is written in "akramanī", but the commentators regard these variants as not significantly affecting the meaning.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the person who is tested either with abundance or with hardship. In wealth he believes God honours him because he deserves it; in poverty he believes God humiliates him. They agree that both wealth and poverty are a test, and that true honour before God lies in obedience and piety, not in how much or how little one owns. The opening "kalla" is a rebuke of this belief, and the passage goes on to condemn behaviour: failing to honour the orphan, not urging the feeding of the poor, devouring inheritance greedily, and loving wealth excessively.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree that the rebuke concerns a false standard of honour and humiliation: God grants or restricts provision not as favour or contempt, but to test gratitude and patience. Al-Zamakhshari suggests the reproach may target the saying "my Lord honoured me" when it implies that one deserved it, and he stresses the attitude of the person. Al-Razi links the error to denial of the resurrection, while Ibn Juzayy notes that the believer who forgets the afterlife is also at risk.

On readings, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi report that "faqadara" may be read with or without doubling the dal, meaning either to restrict or to give just enough. Al-Tabari considers the variant readings of "tahuddun" and "yahuddun" all sound in meaning. The sense of "lamman" varies: a voracious eating, gathering the shares of others, or devouring the inheritance of the weak, though most report that the inheritance is the one from which women and children were excluded.

In this verse God rejects the idea that abundance of wealth is a sign of honour and its lack a sign of contempt. The opening "No!" (kalla) rejects this belief, and the verse then moves to a graver fault: these people do not honour the orphan. Most commentators read "but" (bal) as shifting from blaming a statement to blaming a deed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that wealth and poverty are a trial set by God, and that true honour lies in obedience. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that neglecting the orphan includes not treating him kindly and not giving him his share of inheritance, a view supported by al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya.

The refusal to urge the feeding of the poor, the commentators say, means not encouraging others to help them. The readings differ here, with a form using ta and no alif, a form with ya, or a form with alif; al-Tabari judges all three correct in meaning.

The commentators agree that "al-turath" means the inheritance, and that "aklan lamman" means eating greedily until nothing is left. Al-Hasan and al-Mawardi take it to mean taking one's own share and that of others, Mujahid to mean devouring, and Ibn Zayd reports that the people of pre-Islamic ignorance did not pass inheritance to women or children. For "hubban jamman", Ibn 'Abbas explains it as abundant love, and al-Hasan as mixing the lawful with the unlawful.

The passage ends with a warning: on the Day of Judgment the earth will be crushed, the command of God will come, Hell will be brought forward, and man will remember and wish he had done good for his life.

This passage of Surat al-Fajr describes a common assumption: that wealth is a sign of God's honour and poverty a sign of His contempt. God replies with "No": wealth and poverty are a test, not a measure of a person's worth. The verse then turns to what people actually do: they do not honour the orphan, they do not urge one another to feed the needy, they devour inheritance, combining their own share with that of others, and they love wealth with an intense love. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree that these deeds are blameworthy. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, quoting Qatada, state that true honour lies in obedience and humiliation in disobedience. The commentators differ on the meaning of "lamman": al-Suddi says it means greedy or intense, al-Hasan and Abu 'Ubayda say it means gathering together lawful and unlawful wealth, Mujahid says it means swallowing up, and Ibn Zayd says it means taking one's own share and that of others without discrimination; Ibn Zayd adds that they did not pass inheritance on to women or children. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Zamakhshari read the act as hoarding and refusing to share. Al-Tabari judges the various readings of the verbs (tuhadduna, yahuddun, tahadduna) to be all valid in meaning, without preferring one. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy stress that the central fault is the attachment to property. Some, such as al-Baghawi, link the verse to Umayya ibn Khalaf, though this is not accepted by all. The general lesson is that real worth before God lies in gratitude, patience and generosity, not in the amount of wealth one possesses.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a passage criticising the person who takes wealth as a sign of God's honour and poverty as a sign of humiliation; God answers with 'No' (kalla) and then denounces what such people actually do: not honouring the orphan and not urging the feeding of the needy. As for 'you devour the inheritance greedily' (akkan lamman), al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as eating up everything without leaving anything, including the shares of others. Al-Hasan, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Nasafi add that the pre-Islamic Arabs withheld inheritance from women and children, swallowing their portion along with their own. Ibn Zayd broadens the meaning: one eats without distinguishing what is lawful from what is unlawful, whether it belongs to him or to others. Mujahid glosses 'lamm' as devouring completely, while al-Mawardi lists several senses including gathering together. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan report the view that the verse targets an heir who squanders wealth he did not earn, though Abu Hayyan considers this reading ill-suited to the context. On 'you love wealth with an excessive love' (hubban jamman), Ibn Abbas takes it as abundance, whereas al-Hasan understands it as accumulating both lawful and unlawful gain. The readings of the verbs vary between the second and third person, and al-Tabari holds that all the recognised readings are valid and convey compatible meanings. In short, the commentators agree in condemning the combination of seizing others' rights and an excessive attachment to wealth.

This verse describes the person absorbed in worldly life, who loves wealth with an intense and excessive love. The commentators explain the word jamman as meaning abundant or intense. Al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd render it as intense or great, and al-Tabari cites an Arabic line of poetry to clarify the word. They agree that the verse is a rebuke to those who put the gathering of wealth before what God has commanded them. It follows on from the preceding verses, which reject the view that wealth is a sign of God's honour and poverty a sign of humiliation. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy explain this love as greed combined with withholding what is owed. Al-Hasan understands it as gathering lawful and unlawful wealth together, while al-Mawardi offers a third reading: loving to hoard wealth without benefiting from it. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur stress that such attachment leads to stinginess and to depriving the needy. Al-Sam'ani notes a difference of recitation: the form with the letter ya is read as narrative, the form with ta as direct address. Ibn Sa'di links this fault to a weakness of resolve that looks only at one's own desires. The commentators agree on the general sense, and their differences concern mainly how greed and its forms should be understood.

This passage says that matters are not as the man preoccupied with wealth imagines. When the earth is shaken and crushed, shock after shock, until mountains and buildings are broken and levelled, and when the command and judgment of God come, and the angels descend rank after rank, then the human being will remember what he neglected. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy, agree that the crushing means breaking and levelling, and that the repetition signifies totality and succession. They differ on the coming of the Lord: al-Hasan and others take it as the coming of His command and decree, al-Kalbi speaks of a descent, while al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari read it as an image of the manifestation of His power. Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Uthaymin urge believing in it without modality. Most report that Hell will be brought forward, led by seventy thousand reins, as narrated from Ibn Mas'ud. As for the man who will remember, al-Tabari and al-Mawardi understand it as repentance or awareness of what one did, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi stress that this remembrance will then be of no benefit. The wish to have advanced good deeds for one's life refers, according to the commentators, either to the life to come or to earthly life. Finally, the reading of the verbs with kasra is the majority reading, while al-Kisa'i reads them with fatha.

Verse 89:22 describes the Day of Judgment, when the earth is leveled, the Lord's command and judgment come to separate people, angels descend row upon row, and Hell is brought forward. Commentators agree that the verse depicts the terror of that day, that the angels surround creation rank after rank, and that Hell is presented and made visible. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the coming of the Lord means the coming of His command and judgment, while Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari keep the literal sense of coming to judge. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi read it as an image of the manifestation of God's power, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report hadiths about seventy thousand reins for Hell, each held by seventy thousand angels. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also cite these narrations, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that Hell's coming is a figure for its being made visible. On the verse's sequence, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the remembering of man and the phrase 'and how can remembrance benefit him' refer to his repentance coming too late, while al-Mawardi reports two views: that he repents, or that he recalls what he did in the world. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi add that the man may be a disbeliever in general or a specific person. None of the commentaries judges between these readings.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when Hell will be brought forth, led by seventy thousand reins, each held by seventy thousand angels. On that day man will remember what he neglected, but how will remembrance benefit him when the time for action has passed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as a recollection of his deeds and a reckoning, while al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur take it to mean that remembrance no longer helps, the question being a denial. Al-Mawardi reports that some held it to be a repentance that will not be accepted, a view al-Razi supports in his discussion with the Mu'tazilites. All agree that it is no longer the time for repentance or good works, and that the person meant is the heedless unbeliever. The names proposed for him (Umayya ibn Khalaf, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, 'Utba ibn Rabi'a) remain uncertain, and Ibn 'Atiyya takes the word to mean mankind in general. Readers differ on 'yu'adhdhibu' and 'yuthiqu': the majority reading with kasra refers to God, while al-Kisa'i's reading with fatha refers to the man. Ibn Kathir and Qurtubi report, citing a hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, that Hell will be brought forth in this way. The general lesson is a warning against heedlessness before the opportunity to act is lost.

This verse describes what the human being will say on the Day of Resurrection, when he sees its terrors and Hell is brought forward, remembering his negligence and wishing he had sent ahead good deeds for his life. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'for my life' (li-hayati). Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy understand it as the eternal future life without death, while Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak take it as the life of this world, meaning 'during my life'. All agree that remembrance will be of no benefit on that day and that the wish springs from regret. Regarding the reading of 'yu'adhdhibu' and 'yuthiqu' with kasra, the majority reading, al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj take the pronoun to refer to God, so that none takes charge of His punishment or His bonds. Al-Kisa'i and those who read with fatha, including Abu 'Amr late in life, refer it to the man in question, meaning no one will be punished as he is. Some reports identify the 'human' as a specific person such as Umayya ibn Khalaf or 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, while others take it as the disbeliever in general. The soul at rest (al-nafs al-mutma'inna) is explained as the believing soul that has submitted and found certainty. Some hold that it is addressed at death, others at resurrection, and the meaning of 'return to your Lord' is likewise disputed, between return to the body and return to God's reward.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when no one can punish as God punishes, nor bind as He binds. The majority reading, with kasra on the dhal and the tha’, makes these verbs refer to God: no one takes charge of His punishment or His bonds, and His chastisement surpasses any torment of this world. Al-Tabari regards this reading as the correct one, and Ibn ‘Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi follow it, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy likewise making the pronoun refer to God. A reading with fatha, attributed to al-Kisa’i and Ya‘qub and to a report from the Prophet, makes the pronouns refer to the disbeliever: no one punishes as he is punished, nor binds as he is bound. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi mention that this refers to a specific disbeliever, named by some as Umayya ibn Khalaf or Ubayy ibn Khalaf, while Abu ‘Ubayda considered the kasra reading weak, since no one but God punishes on that day. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the soul at rest is the believer who is certain of God’s promise, submissive and content. They agree that she is addressed: “O soul at rest, return to your Lord, content and well-pleasing, enter among My servants and enter My Garden.” Scholars differ on when this is said. Abu Salih and Ibn Kathir place it at death, while Ibn ‘Abbas and Ikrima place it at resurrection, and al-Tabari leans toward the latter.

The commentators place this verse within their description of the terrors of the Last Day: the earth is crushed, God comes to judge, Hell is brought forward, and the heedless person then remembers what he did and regrets not having sent forward good deeds for his everlasting life. As for the phrase 'None punishes as He punishes, and none binds as He binds,' the majority reading, with a kasra on the dhal and the tha', refers to God: no one can inflict a punishment or bonds comparable to His, as Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada say, or no one but Him holds that power, as al-Razi and others note. Al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read with fatha, which refers to the disbelieving man mentioned: none punishes as this disbeliever is punished, and none binds as he is bound. Some identify him as Ubayy ibn Khalaf or Umayya ibn Khalaf, and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim prefer this reading. Al-Tabari keeps the majority reading on the basis of the consensus of the readers. Regarding 'O soul at peace,' the exegetes understand it as the believing soul, certain, content with God's decree and trusting His promise, to which it is said: 'Return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing, enter among My servants and enter My Paradise.' Scholars differ on when this is said and on the meaning of 'return': for Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and al-Dahhak it is the return of the soul to the body at resurrection, while Abu Salih takes it to refer to the moment of death; al-Tabari favours the first view. Ibn al-Qayyim reconciles the two by saying that the address begins at death and is completed on the Day of Resurrection.

God addresses in this verse the soul at rest, and the commentators agree that it means the believing soul that has settled in trust with its Lord and believed His promise, with neither doubt nor fear troubling it. Mujahid explains it as the soul that knew God to be its Lord and submitted firmly to His command; Qatada and al-Hasan say it is the one that affirms what God promised; 'Ata' says it is content with God's decree; al-Kalbi says it is safe from God's punishment. Ibn 'Abbas says it is the believing soul, and some note that the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, "the secure and tranquil soul", supports the sense of safety. As to when this address is made, opinions differ: most, including Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Salih and Ibn Zayd, hold that it is at death, and a hadith of the Prophet to Abu Bakr is cited for this; others, such as 'Ikrima, 'Ata' and al-Dahhak, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, say it is at the resurrection when souls return to their bodies, a view al-Tabari preferred, while Ibn Kathir considered the first the more apparent. Most hold that the Paradise meant is the abode of eternity, and that "among My servants" means among the righteous; Ibn 'Abbas read "in My servant", which some take as referring to the body. Several report that the verse was revealed concerning particular companions such as Hamza or 'Uthman, but the majority holds it to be general for every tranquil believing soul.

This verse addresses the tranquil soul, meaning the believing soul that has become certain in faith and settled in trust of God's promise, and tells it to return to its Lord, content with what it has been given and pleasing to Him. The commentators agree that this refers to the believing soul that is serene and convinced, although they phrase its description differently. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Hasan describe it as the soul that affirms and believes, al-Mujahid as the one that accepts God's decree, turns back to Him and is humble, and al-Kalbi as the one safe from God's punishment. There is disagreement over when this call is made. Most scholars, including Ibn Zayd, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, say it is at death, relying on the report about Abu Bakr. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, 'Ata' and al-Dahhak hold that it is at the resurrection, when souls return to their bodies, while al-Hasan places it at the moment God decides to take the soul. Al-Tabari prefers the resurrection view, because of the following words: enter among My servants and enter My Paradise. On the meaning of returning to the Lord, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it as returning to the body, al-Hasan as returning to God's reward and honour, and Abu Salih as returning to God at death. Entering among My servants means, for most, joining the company of the righteous; al-Dahhak understands it as obedience to God, and al-Sudi as being with His servants. Most exegetes take the Paradise mentioned to be the abode of eternity, the home of the righteous. Some report that the verse was revealed about Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, others about 'Uthman or Khubayb ibn 'Adi, but Ibn Kathir holds that its ruling applies generally to all tranquil believers.

This verse addresses the soul that is believing and at peace, certain of the truth and tranquil in God's promise. It is told to return to its Lord, content with what it has received and pleasing to Him, and then to enter among His righteous servants and into His Paradise. Most commentators, such as Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan and al-Tabari, understand al-mutma'inna as the believer who is certain and has no doubt, and most hold that the verse applies to every sincere soul, although some reports link it to Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Uthman or Khubayb ibn Adi. Some mention a reading attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-nafs al-amina, the secure soul. As to when these words are spoken, Ibn Abbas, Abu Salih and Ibn Kathir place it at death, citing the hadith addressed to Abu Bakr, while al-Tabari, in another view, places it at the resurrection when souls return to their bodies. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Qayyim reconcile both views. On the phrase return to your Lord, some say to His reward, others to the body, others to His appointed time. On enter among My servants, most take it as the righteous servants, Dahhak takes it as obedience, and others, following Ibn Abbas's reading my servant, take it as the body. Al-Tabari adopts that last reading, but most prefer the first meaning.

God addresses the tranquil soul of the believer, bidding it return to its Lord, content and pleasing to Him, to enter among His righteous servants and to enter His Paradise. The commentators agree that the tranquil soul is the one that is certain and settled in the truth, that believes God's promise, and that neither doubt nor fear can unsettle. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir note that the plainest meaning is the believing soul that accepts God's decree. On when this is said, they differ: Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak and al-Tabari hold that it is said at the resurrection, when souls are returned to bodies, while Abu Salih, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd hold that it is said at death. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi consider that it may apply at death, at resurrection and on entry into Paradise. The 'return to the Lord' is understood either as a return to the body, or as a return to God's reward or judgment. Some read 'My servant' in the singular, which some linked to the body. Al-Wahidi and others report occasions of revelation (Hamza, Khubayb ibn 'Adi, 'Uthman), but most scholars stress that the general wording matters more than the specific cause. Paradise is, for most, the abode of eternity prepared for the righteous.
